explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Ishmael and his ten men come to Gedaliah at Mizpah, and they eat a meal together there (Jeremiah 41:1). Ishmael was a member of the royal family and one of the king's chief officers. I think that meal had to be the quietest one ever served.

The text says the opposite, friend. Ishmael came with ten men to Gedaliah at Mizpah, "…and they ate a meal together there." (Jeremiah 41:1) Nobody stormed in swinging. They sat down and ate first, and that's what makes the next verse land so hard.

That's the one, baker. Ishmael killed "…the Chaldean soldiers who were there." along with the Jews who were with Gedaliah (Jeremiah 41:3). Gedaliah was the one whom the king of Babylon had appointed to govern the land (Jeremiah 41:2). That detail matters later in this story.

Close on the map, but not the ones at Mizpah. The text says Ishmael killed the Chaldean soldiers who were there (Jeremiah 41:3). Egypt does come up later, but it's not the soldiers' home team here. Hang onto that word, friend, because it comes back.
The Philistines are a good guess for a soldier question, baker. But the text names the Chaldean soldiers at Mizpah as the ones Ishmael killed (Jeremiah 41:3). No Philistines anywhere in this scene.

Right, baker. The eighty men were carrying grain offerings and frankincense "…for the house of the LORD." (Jeremiah 41:5) They had shaved their beards, torn their clothes and cut themselves, and they still made the trip with offerings in their hands. I think that tells you how much it mattered to them.

Babylon's palace is a long walk from Shechem, friend. The offerings were "…for the house of the LORD." (Jeremiah 41:5) These men came from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria, carrying grain offerings and frankincense toward the LORD's house.

Not Baal, baker. The text says the grain offerings and frankincense were for "…the house of the LORD." (Jeremiah 41:5) These men came from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria, and they were bringing their offerings to the LORD's house.

That's it, baker. Ishmael "…went out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he went." (Jeremiah 41:6) The text tells us what he did, and it doesn't say why he did it. What he did to those men next is heavy.
No laughing here, friend. The text says Ishmael went out "…weeping as he went." (Jeremiah 41:6) This is a heavy part of the story. Gedaliah already lies dead at this point (Jeremiah 41:2).

No songs on this road, baker. Ishmael went out to meet the eighty men "…weeping as he went." (Jeremiah 41:6) That's a sad scene even before the next verse. The eighty men came on the second day after Gedaliah was murdered (Jeremiah 41:4).

explanations.answer: Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Ishmael said, "Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam." (Jeremiah 41:6) Gedaliah was already dead, and the eighty men didn't know it, since the text says no one yet knew (Jeremiah 41:4). The invitation sounded friendly, and that's what makes it so chilling.

explanations.answer: Turn back to your homes now
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. What Ishmael actually said was, "Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam." (Jeremiah 41:6) He didn't tell them to turn back. He called them toward Gedaliah, who was already dead, and when they came into the city, Ishmael and his men slaughtered them (Jeremiah 41:7).

Not quite, baker. The eighty men were already headed toward the house of the LORD (Jeremiah 41:5), so Ishmael didn't point them to Jerusalem. He said, "Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam." (Jeremiah 41:6) In the city, Ishmael and his men slaughtered them and threw them into a cistern, though ten were spared (Jeremiah 41:7-8).

Not this time, friend. Ten of the men told Ishmael, "Do not kill us, for we have hidden treasure in the field…" The text says "So he refrained from killing them with the others." (Jeremiah 41:8) They spoke up and were spared. The other men weren't so fortunate.

Right, baker. The ten men said they had hidden treasure in the field, and the text says "So he refrained from killing them with the others." (Jeremiah 41:8) The ten were spared, while the others were slaughtered and thrown into a cistern (Jeremiah 41:7). This is a heavy part of the story.

That's right, baker. Ishmael "…set off to cross over to the Ammonites." (Jeremiah 41:10) He took captive all the remnant of the people of Mizpah, including the daughters of the king. He was taking them away from Mizpah.

Good guess on a long trip, friend, but no. The text says Ishmael "…set off to cross over to the Ammonites." (Jeremiah 41:10) He wasn't headed to Damascus. He was taking his captives out of Mizpah toward the Ammonites.
Moab is a good guess, baker, but it's not the one here. The text says Ishmael "…set off to cross over to the Ammonites." (Jeremiah 41:10) Moab doesn't come up in this passage.

explanations.answer: Near the great pool in Gibeon
explanations.explanation: That's the spot, baker. Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the armies with him took all their men and went to fight Ishmael, and they "…found him near the great pool in Gibeon." (Jeremiah 41:12) Gibeon is where they caught up with him.

The Jordan is a fair guess, friend, but it's not the place named. The text says Johanan's men found him "…near the great pool in Gibeon." (Jeremiah 41:12) Ishmael later escaped from Johanan with eight of his men and went to the Ammonites (Jeremiah 41:15).

Not Jerusalem, baker. The text says they found Ishmael "…near the great pool in Gibeon." (Jeremiah 41:12) He was still on his way to the Ammonites with his captives when Johanan caught up. Gibeon is where they finally met.

Yes, baker, they rejoiced. The text says, "When all the people with Ishmael saw Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the army with him, they rejoiced…" (Jeremiah 41:13) Then all the people Ishmael had taken captive at Mizpah turned and went over to Johanan (Jeremiah 41:14). I bet they were glad to see him.

I'd have trembled too, friend, but that's not what the text says. The people with Ishmael "rejoiced" when they saw Johanan and the commanders (Jeremiah 41:13). I think they'd been waiting for someone, anyone, to show up. They got Johanan.

They did move, baker, but they didn't scatter. The text says they "rejoiced," and then they turned and went over to Johanan (Jeremiah 41:13-14). They all headed the same direction, straight toward their rescuers.

Not quite, friend. The text says "…Ishmael son of Nethaniah and eight of his men escaped from Johanan…" (Jeremiah 41:15) He came to Mizpah with ten men (Jeremiah 41:1), so the number here is eight, not ten. Ishmael got away and went to the Ammonites.

Right, baker, the number is eight. "…Ishmael son of Nethaniah and eight of his men escaped from Johanan and went to the Ammonites." (Jeremiah 41:15) He came to Mizpah with ten men (Jeremiah 41:1), so ten isn't the number here. The captives had turned and gone over to Johanan (Jeremiah 41:14).

That's the one, baker. They stayed at Geruth Chimham, near Bethlehem, "…in order to proceed into Egypt" (Jeremiah 41:17) The text says they planned to go, and the next verse tells us why they wanted out. Remember this word, because it matters for what comes next.

Edom is a neighbor, friend, but it's not their plan. The text says they stayed at Geruth Chimham "…in order to proceed into Egypt" (Jeremiah 41:17) Egypt was the destination in their minds. They just hadn't left yet.
Not Assyria, baker. Johanan and the people stopped at Geruth Chimham, near Bethlehem, "…in order to proceed into Egypt" (Jeremiah 41:17). Assyria isn't in this passage at all. Egypt was the plan.

explanations.answer: Ishmael killed the governor Babylon appointed
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker, that's the reason. "…they were afraid of the Chaldeans because Ishmael son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land." (Jeremiah 41:18) Ishmael did the killing, and the people were the ones who felt the fear. They wanted to escape the Chaldeans.

Good memory on Johanan, friend, but this isn't it. He took his men and went to fight Ishmael (Jeremiah 41:12). The people feared the Chaldeans "…because Ishmael son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land." (Jeremiah 41:18)

explanations.answer: The people stopped serving Babylon's king
explanations.explanation: That's not what this passage says, baker. The text gives this reason: "…Ishmael son of Nethaniah had struck down Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land." (Jeremiah 41:18) Nothing here mentions the people stopping their service. The fear came because of what Ishmael did.
